title: Values Field Creation
opening: Make a value easier to live through the conditions around an action. Test what those conditions actually reward.

labels.comparison: The same objection, two different responses
labels.claim: Our instructions work for every new learner.
labels.objection: A new learner gets stuck at step two and cannot finish.
labels.inquiryGroup: Inquiry that can revise a claim
labels.praiseResult: The group protects agreement. The claim stays broad, so the failed step does not change what they say or do.
labels.inquiryResult: The group asks what the failed step shows. It narrows the claim and tests a clearer step two; correction changes the next action.
labels.solitude: Solo work can be useful when concentration matters. A private evidence note and a later check can support the same value without adding social contact.
labels.groupModeHelp: Use recurring practice with room for an objection to change the claim. Participation stays voluntary.
labels.soloModeHelp: Use a focused setting and a written counterexample check. No meeting or contact is needed.
labels.setting: Setting or routine that makes the conduct easier
labels.feedback: How you will notice, record, or respond to correction
labels.observationPrompt: Imagine the same kind of counterexample reaches this practice. What should happen next?
labels.observationGroup: A participant can raise an objection; the group can revise a claim and try a changed action.
labels.observationSolo: Write down the counterexample, adjust the claim or practice, and check the next attempt when concentration allows.
labels.observationQuestion: What would show that the conduct is becoming easier or more reliable? What condition would you change if the arrangement rewarded appearances instead?
labels.private: This practice stays private to you. Nothing is sent to or scheduled with another person.
labels.tooLong: Shorten the arrangement to 2,000 characters or fewer. Your full draft remains here; nothing was saved.
labels.sourceExcerpt: “Identify people and settings that support the conduct. Arrange recurring contact, feedback or shared practice so the value has conditions in which to be lived.”
labels.sourceLocator: Supplied recovered manuscript, p. 41 (82-page edition). This lesson lets you design and rehearse an arrangement locally; it does not contact anyone.
labels.example: A name is not the interaction
labels.exampleBody: Calling a group “truth-seeking” proves nothing about its conduct. If members praise every claim and objections change nothing, agreement is being reinforced. A useful inquiry practice lets a concrete objection alter what the group says or tries. A solo evidence note can be a better fit when the work needs concentration.

source.excerpt: Identify people and settings that support the conduct. Arrange recurring contact, feedback or shared practice so the value has conditions in which to be lived.
source.boundary: “Field” refers to the conditions around conduct, not an invisible force. Supportive conditions do not replace participation or prove an outcome. A group that protects agreement from correction does not support truth-seeking. Solitude may fit work that needs concentration.

assessment.guidedQuestion: Everyone agrees with you. Does that establish a supportive truth-seeking setting?
assessment.learnerCheck: Can you describe the actual interactions that support the value?
assessment.outcomeCheck: Does the arrangement improve conduct while preserving honest correction and workable commitments?
assessment.changeAccount: If belonging becomes conditional on agreement, reconsider the arrangement.
